blocks.title: Air Quality Index
blocks.text: Air quality is measured by the Air Quality Index (AQI), a measure of the concentrations of pollutants in the air at a particular location. When air quality is good the air is clear and contains only small amounts of solid particles and chemical pollutants; poor air quality, with high levels, is often hazy and dangerous to health and the environment.

An AQI value under 50 is considered good: it is safe to spend time outdoors without risk to health. An AQI over 300 is hazardous. Children under 18, adults over 65 and people with chronic heart and lung disease are at high risk, and outdoor workers are at higher risk because of prolonged exposure.

blocks.long_description: The Air Quality Index turns pollutant concentrations into six colour bands from good to hazardous, with children, the elderly, the sick and outdoor workers most at risk. Particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide inflame the airways and over time cause asthma, bronchitis, heart disease and cancer. Nephelometers, continuous emission monitors, fixed stations and satellites measure the pollutants, and a hypothesis such as higher PM2.5 at rush hour is tested by planned sampling and analysis. Catalytic converters, particulate filters, selective catalytic reduction and scrubbers cut emissions at the source, backed in Pakistan by the Environmental Protection Act, national quality standards and the Punjab amendment, and by measures from cleaner fuels to smog control, while pollution's costs fall on productivity, crops, the vulnerable and on politics across borders.
